Wrapper methods

Source: vignettes/articles/wrappers.Rmd
wrappers.Rmd

A wrapper method fits a model to many candidate subsets of the predictors and keeps the subset that model scores best. Because it refits the model for each candidate, a wrapper costs far more than a filter, and its answer only holds for the model family it wraps: the subset a random forest prefers can differ from the one a linear model prefers. The search also uses the data to pick a winner, so the winner’s own score is optimistic. Each section below names the number that is computed on rows the search never saw; Validation and leakage has the full table of held-out and optimistic quantities.

The five wrappers answer different questions:

  • fs_recursivefeature() and fs_svm() rank the predictors with one model and keep the subset size whose cross-validated performance is best.
  • fs_boruta() looks for every predictor that carries any information about the outcome, then by default keeps only the most important member of each correlated group.
  • fs_stepwise() keeps the terms that lower AIC in a linear regression.
  • fs_bayes() compares Bayesian models on every candidate subset by approximate leave-one-out cross-validation.

Choosing a method compares them with the filter and embedded methods.

fs_recursivefeature()

Recursive feature elimination (RFE) fits a model on all predictors, ranks them by the model’s importance, and refits on the top-ranked subset of each candidate size. fs_recursivefeature() wraps caret::rfe(). It first makes a stratified train/test split (train_ratio = 0.8 by default), runs the elimination on the training rows, lets cross-validation choose the subset size, and then scores the result on the test rows.

rfe <- fs_recursivefeature(
  iris, "Species",
  sizes = 1:4,
  rfe_control = list(method = "cv", number = 5),
  seed = 1
)
selected(rfe)
#> [1] "Petal.Width"  "Petal.Length"
rfe$details$optimal_size
#> [1] 2
rfe$details$test_metrics         # held out: the honest estimate
#>  Accuracy     Kappa 
#> 0.9666667 0.9500000
rfe$details$resampling_results   # inside the training rows
#>   Variables  Accuracy Kappa AccuracySD    KappaSD
#> 1         1 0.9333333 0.900  0.0372678 0.05590170
#> 2         2 0.9666667 0.950  0.0186339 0.02795085
#> 3         3 0.9500000 0.925  0.0186339 0.02795085
#> 4         4 0.9500000 0.925  0.0186339 0.02795085

On iris the search keeps two predictors, Petal.Width and Petal.Length, with a cross-validated accuracy of 0.967 at size 2, against 0.933 for one predictor and 0.950 for three or four. The held-out accuracy on the 30 test rows is also 0.967.

Only details$test_metrics is a held-out estimate. resampling_results is computed inside the training rows, and the size is chosen as the best row of that table, so the winning row’s score is optimistic. The same applies to model$results when you set return_final_model = TRUE: that tuning resampling runs on features that were already selected on the same rows.

By default the elimination fits random forests (caret::rfFuncs). To match the model you intend to use, pass another caret function set, for example rfe_control = list(method = "cv", number = 5, functions = caret::lmFuncs) for linear regression. A factor, character, or logical target is treated as classification and anything else as regression. Predictors with missing values are an error, so impute or drop them first. Factor predictors are passed to the model as they are unless you set handle_categorical = TRUE, which one-hot encodes them with an encoder fitted on the training rows only. return_final_model = TRUE also trains a caret model (model_method, default "rf") on the selected features.

The regression metrics are caret’s RMSE, Rsquared, and MAE. caret’s Rsquared is the squared correlation between predictions and observations, not 1 - SSE/SST, so it is never negative and ignores bias. It cannot be compared with an R2 defined as 1 - SSE/SST, such as the one fs_randomforest() reports.

fs_svm()

fs_svm() trains a support vector machine through caret and kernlab, and with feature_select = TRUE it selects features first. The default selector is SVM-RFE (Guyon et al., 2002): fit a linear SVM on the centered and scaled training data, rank the features by their squared weight w^2, drop the weakest, and refit, until one feature is left. The order of elimination is the ranking, so the feature removed last ranks first. Use it when you want the selector and the final model to come from the same family.

sv <- fs_svm(
  iris, "Species",
  task = "classification",
  kernel = "linear",
  tune_grid = data.frame(C = c(0.1, 1)),
  feature_select = TRUE,
  select_method = "svm_rfe",
  nfolds = 5,
  seed = 1
)
selected(sv)
#> [1] "Petal.Width"
sv$details$selection$ranking
#> [1] "Petal.Width"  "Petal.Length" "Sepal.Width"  "Sepal.Length"
sv$details$performance$overall[c("Accuracy", "Kappa")]
#>  Accuracy     Kappa 
#> 0.9333333 0.9000000

Here SVM-RFE ranks Petal.Width first and keeps it alone. The tuned SVM on that one feature classifies 0.933 of the test rows correctly.

You must state task explicitly; fs_svm() does not guess it from the target. SVM-RFE needs kernel = "linear", because the ranking uses the primal weight vector, which exists only for a linear kernel. For a radial or polynomial kernel, use select_method = "rf_rfe", which screens with random forests instead. Without n_features, cross-validation chooses how many features to keep from a short ladder of sizes: the powers of two up to the number of features plus the full size, at most six sizes, always including 1. Missing values in the target or predictors are an error.

Selection runs on the training split (train_ratio = 0.7 by default), and details$performance comes from the untouched test split, so it is the honest estimate. Two other numbers are optimistic. Each entry of details$selection$size_scores is a nested cross-validation estimate for its own size, but the chosen size is the best of up to six noisy estimates. And with feature_select = TRUE, the final model’s tuning cross-validation (sv$model$results, which is what printing sv$model shows) reuses the training rows the selector already used, so on pure noise it can approach perfect accuracy. For regression, Rsquared in details$performance is caret’s squared correlation, as for fs_recursivefeature().

Selection works on the dummy-encoded predictors, so each level of a factor is selected or dropped on its own. On wide data the elimination is slow, because it refits the SVM at every step; screen first with a filter such as fs_supervised().

fs_boruta()

fs_boruta() asks which features carry any information about the outcome, rather than which small subset predicts best. Boruta (Kursa and Rudnicki, 2010) adds a shuffled “shadow” copy of every feature, grows random forests, and confirms each feature whose importance beats the best shadow significantly more often than chance. Boruta itself confirms every informative feature, redundant ones included, which helps when you want to understand a data set and hurts when you want a compact model. featR adds a pruning step on top: with the default cutoff_cor = 0.7, it keeps only the most important member of each group of confirmed features correlated above 0.7. A factor target is treated as classification and a numeric one as regression. Missing values are an error.

The example below has one real predictor (signal), a noisy copy of it (echo), and two predictors generated independently of y.

set.seed(3)
bd <- data.frame(
  signal  = rnorm(150),
  noise1  = rnorm(150),
  noise2  = rnorm(150)
)
bd$echo <- bd$signal + rnorm(150, sd = 0.2)
bd$y <- factor(ifelse(bd$signal + rnorm(150, sd = 0.5) > 0, "a", "b"))

bo <- fs_boruta(bd, "y", maxRuns = 50, cutoff_cor = NULL, seed = 1)
bo$details$decisions
#>    signal    noise1    noise2      echo 
#> Confirmed  Rejected Confirmed Confirmed 
#> Levels: Tentative Confirmed Rejected
selected(bo)
#> [1] "signal" "noise2" "echo"

# featR addition: within each correlated group, keep the most important member
selected(fs_boruta(bd, "y", maxRuns = 50, cutoff_cor = 0.7, seed = 1))
#> [1] "signal" "noise2"

The first call turns off featR’s correlation pruning, so signal and echo can both be confirmed. The second call uses the default cutoff_cor = 0.7 and keeps only the more important of the two.

noise2 is confirmed too, although it has nothing to do with y. Two things combine here. In this particular sample noise2 happens to carry some random-forest importance: Boruta on its own leaves it Tentative after 50 runs and confirms it in two of three seeds after 250. Then resolve_tentative = TRUE (the default) settles every feature still undecided with Boruta::TentativeRoughFix(). That function confirms a feature whenever its median importance beats the median of the best shadow, a weaker test than the one used during the run. In a simulation of 20 data sets with one real and three pure-noise predictors (150 rows, 100 runs each), Boruta alone confirmed 5% of the noise features, and 8.3% after the rough fix.

So Boruta limits false discoveries but does not eliminate them. When they are costly, set resolve_tentative = FALSE, inspect details$decisions, raise maxRuns (default 250), and validate the confirmed set on held-out data. Results vary from run to run unless you pass seed.

fs_stepwise()

Stepwise regression adds or removes one term at a time, keeping each move that lowers AIC. fs_stepwise() runs MASS::stepAIC() on a linear regression of the target on every other column. It is the cheapest wrapper in featR, it is deterministic (there is no seed argument), and it returns an ordinary lm.

st <- fs_stepwise(mtcars, "mpg", direction = "both")
selected(st)
#> [1] "wt"   "qsec" "am"
st$scores
#>       wt     qsec       am 
#> 5.506882 4.246676 2.080819

On mtcars the search keeps wt, qsec, and am. The scores are absolute t statistics: 5.51, 4.25, and 2.08.

Those t statistics, and the p-values in details$coefficients, are computed on the same data that drove the search, so they are biased toward significance. Use them to order the retained terms, not for inference. The search is also greedy, so it can miss the AIC-best subset, and unstable, so small changes to the data can change the answer. Pass k = log(nrow(data)) to use BIC, which usually keeps fewer terms.

The target must be numeric. Rows with a missing value in any column are dropped with a warning before the search, because stepAIC() can only compare models fitted on the same rows. To refit the returned model with update(), pass the data explicitly, for example update(st$model, . ~ . - am, data = mtcars).

fs_bayes()

fs_bayes() fits a brms model for every candidate subset of predictors and compares them by approximate leave-one-out cross-validation (PSIS-LOO; Vehtari et al., 2017) with loo::loo_compare(). The default rule = "1se" picks the smallest subset whose expected log predictive density (elpd) is within one standard error of the best; rule = "best" takes the maximum. The model family comes from brm_family, for example stats::gaussian() (the default) or brms::bernoulli(). Rows with a missing value in the target, any candidate predictor, or date_col are dropped before fitting.

res <- fs_bayes(
  mtcars, "mpg",
  predictors = c("wt", "hp", "qsec"),
  brm_args = list(chains = 2, iter = 1000, seed = 1),
  seed = 1
)
selected(res)
res$details$loo_comparison

This example is not run here, because each candidate model compiles and samples its own Stan program, which needs brms, loo, and a working C++ toolchain. It is the most expensive method in featR: with p candidates it fits 2^p - 1 models, seven for the three predictors above. Bound the search with max_comb_size or sample_combinations.

None of the numbers it returns is a held-out estimate. details$mae and details$rmse are in-sample. details$best_elpd would be roughly unbiased for a single fixed model, but it belongs to the model that won a search over up to 2^p - 1 candidates, so it is optimistic (selection-induced bias; Piironen and Vehtari, 2017), and so are the differences in details$loo_comparison. Posterior intervals from the returned model are post-selection. To judge the chosen subset, use data the search did not see, or repeat the whole search inside an outer cross-validation.

References

Guyon, I., Weston, J., Barnhill, S. and Vapnik, V. (2002). Gene selection for cancer classification using support vector machines. Machine Learning 46, 389–422. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1012487302797

Kursa, M. B. and Rudnicki, W. R. (2010). Feature selection with the Boruta package. Journal of Statistical Software 36(11). https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v036.i11

Piironen, J. and Vehtari, A. (2017). Comparison of Bayesian predictive methods for model selection. Statistics and Computing 27, 711–735. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11222-016-9649-y

Vehtari, A., Gelman, A. and Gabry, J. (2017). Practical Bayesian model evaluation using leave-one-out cross-validation and WAIC. Statistics and Computing 27, 1413–1432. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11222-016-9696-4
